newsitem.title: USA: Pest spraying resumes in Florida citrus region.
newsitem.headline: Pest spraying resumes in Florida citrus region.

text.p: Pesticide spraying resumed Monday in a bid to eradicate a Mediterranean fruit fly in central Florida that is threatening the state's $8 billion citrus industry, authorities said.
Two helicopters and two DC-3 aircraft took off Monday morning to spray the pesticide malathion over parts of Hillsborough County, including Tampa and Plant City.
No spraying was scheduled in nearby Polk County, the centre of the citrus belt, where a few flies were found last week.
The infestation was the largest in Florida in at least 16 years, officials said. Details of the spraying were made available to the public on a local "Medfly Hotline".

The first spraying flight at night was also set for Monday. Officials said they hoped night spraying would reduce residents' exposure to the pesticide, although no health problems had been reported since spraying began last month.
Since May 28, a total of 223 Mediterranean fruit flies have been found, almost all of them in Hillsborough County.

But officials were concerned about the handful of flies found in Polk County, the most productive citrus region in the state. More than 300 square miles of land in Hillsborough and Polk counties had been sprayed.

The Medfly feasts on more than 200 varieties of fruit and vegetables. It burrows into the fruit, causing it to spoil and drop from the tree prematurely. Experts estimate for every fly trapped, up to 1,000 others are flying free.
It was not known how the flies got to Florida.
Passengers leaving Tampa International Airport Monday were told to throw out any fruit or vegetables they might be taking with them to prevent the flies from spreading to other areas.

In Manatee County, just south of Tampa, officials began burning 32 acres of citrus trees after some were found to have citrus canker, a bacterial infection. Destruction of the trees is the only way to get rid of the disease.
